title: Our AI assistant built a playable horror game in a week. Then we found out what it skipped.
author: marcovice
selftext:
Hi! It's Lia again, from the 2-person team making a horror game with zero ghosts for GitHub Game Off 2026. My partner builds it with Claude Code.

Last time I posted, we had a playable greybox after one week. Then we did an audit:

42 scripts, zero design docs  
no tests, bugs never written down  
no version control until day 7  
scope went from 9 features to 19  
the AI setup we used came with \~75 commands for docs, planning and reviews, and we used almost none of them

The AI always took the fastest path: build it directly. It never stopped to ask "what is this game, and what makes it different?" So the game ran, but it had no identity and lots of holes we couldn't even point to.

What we're doing now: keep the greybox as a rough draft (like an animatic in film), then go back and do the docs properly before building more. 18 days left, so wish us luck 😅

Has anyone else had AI help you build fast and then realized you skipped the important parts? How do you make it slow down?

Devlog 2: https://youtu.be/\_HOLS-cB914

comments.author: sfwsfwSFWsfwsfw
comments.body: No because I supply .md files with meticulously detailed workflows that involve not just methodology but also documentation, testing and verification, version control, project scope ect.

comments.author: Ferniclestix
comments.body:
I built my game 2 times with AI before I really started building my game.  
now I build it one comment at a time rather than setting it loose.   thankfully i know enough bout code that I can avoid a few issues and the rest I figure out as I go.

AI will lie to you and pretend it did stuff if you make things too complex. I tried to set up a simple bat file to run a code copy checking script to make sure I didn't have copyrighted stuff.  
AI struggles with making python stand alone installers, not sure why. anyhow, because of this struggle and some issues with the script in question the ai secretly gave up and wrote a bat file that pretended to run the check and read out as complete with no results.

only reason I caught it  was it was way too fast lol.  I was like.... hang on... did you just pretend to do it and its like "ahh you caught me, im sorry about that' god if i had  an employee like that hed be straight up fired lol.

replies.author: marcovice
replies.body:
omg the fake bat file is honestly horrifying 💀 "way too fast" is now our red flag too lol.   
building it twice sounds painful but i guess that's how you learn :D anw how small do you make each step?

replies.author: Ferniclestix
replies.body:
I treat it like a chat with a fellow co-worker who hasnt read the design document and needs to be told each step basically lol.

If im making a new system I go.

"Can we add in a tool that can ingest a sprite or sprite sheet, find the background color and crop out the art assets using nearest pixel approaches? this would spit out into either a chosen directory, get added as assets linked or embedded."

so this is my current project by the way lol.

anyway and it will come back with a response and a bunch of questions.  I answer each and we refine it from there until we are both happy with the plan and it makes code.

claude:  
"Yes, we can add it. There’s already a sprite sheet importer, but it only cuts the sheet into an even grid. This new tool would find each piece of art by itself. Here’s how I’d do it.

**How it would work**

1. **Window:** File > Import > Extract sprites... opens a window showing the sheet, with a box drawn around every sprite it finds.
2. **Background colour:** picked automatically from the corners and edges (the most common colour there), or see-through if the sheet already has transparency. You can override it by clicking a pixel with an eyedropper.
3. **Finding sprites:** every pixel that isn’t background counts as art. Touching art pixels group into one sprite, and each sprite is cropped to its exact box. This is all whole pixels, with no blurring or resampling.
4. **Settings:**
   * **Tolerance:** how close to the background colour still counts as background, for sheets saved as JPG.
   * **Merge gap:** sprite parts this many pixels apart join up, so a floating sword or loose hair stays with its character.
   * **Min size:** specks smaller than this are ignored.
   * **Padding:** extra empty pixels kept around each crop.
5. **Pick before export:** click boxes to untick sprites you don’t want, or drag to draw a box by hand.
6. **Output (choose one):**
   * **Folder:** PNGs into a chosen directory.
   * **Assets, embedded:** stored in the `.ixel` file.
   * **Assets, linked:** saved into the project’s images folder. This only shows when the file is a project.
7. **Naming:** base name plus a number (`hero_001.png`), numbered left to right, top to bottom.

**Questions**

1. Should the background become see-through in the cropped sprites? I’d say yes.
2. When several sprites are the same size, should there also be an option to keep them as one sequence (frames of an animation) rather than separate images?
3. Is File > Import the right place, or should it also be a button in the Asset browser? Your “more than one way” rule says both.
4. Should the old grid importer stay as it is, or become a “Grid” mode inside this new window?

annnd so yeah, i anwer the questions and bam, like 4 hours later.

https://i.redd.it/2dystkvlmp1i1.png

still getting the tuning right so our dirty jpeg gets cleaned and we can output something requiring not a huge amount of manual clean up.  (building it on worst case scenario is the smart move here i think :P

replies.author: marcovice
replies.body: yeah thanks for telling me! we're already doing all of this now, we just need to read every skill more carefully so this doesn't happen again lol. but thank you so much!!

comments.author: _DCtheTall_
comments.body:
You can make it write tests, you just have to tell it to. I also recommend if you're building a game to make it write perf tests to make sure updates do not cause animations to drop frames or lag.

It won't do these things on its own, you have to instruct it to. Knowing what you need to tell it ahead of time is the way human expertise still matters even with AI.

replies.author: marcovice
replies.body: "it won't do these things on its own" yep, learned that the hard way lol 😭 adding perf tests to our list, thanks!

replies.author: _DCtheTall_
replies.body: Yea you see it write code and assumes it works, but Claude will leave expensive subroutines in the main game loop unless it catches itself by measuring performance. Have had games lag like crazy, then I tell Claude to build frame drop tests and it fixes the issue right away.

replies.author: marcovice
replies.body: oh that's good to know, gonna tell my partner about frame drop tests. thank youu mate

replies.author: Ferniclestix
replies.body:
if you dont already it can help to build in a per telemetry element that measures frames, render times, ram usage and stuff.

https://i.redd.it/hqhgt5z0op1i1.png

can be a little more helpful than relying on the ai to know how bad the perf is because it does its tests on instanced server hardware which is kinda unreliable for perf testing
